core: Classical Greece as a period: conventionally the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, from roughly the end of the Persian Wars (479 BCE) to the death of Alexander the Great (323 BCE)
The polis (independent, self-governing city-state) as the basic political unit, and the contrast between Athens (a democracy) and Sparta (a militarized oligarchy headed by two kings)

Athenian direct democracy for adult male citizens, established by the reforms of Cleisthenes (c. 508 BCE) with the Council of 500 (boule) and the Assembly, and its explicit exclusion of women, enslaved people, and foreign residents (metics) — a 'limited democracy'
The Greco-Persian Wars (OpenStax dates them 492-449 BCE): battles at Marathon (490 BCE), Thermopylae and Salamis (480 BCE), and Plataea (479 BCE); the Delian League (477 BCE) led by Athens
The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) between Athens and its empire and Sparta and its allies, ending in Athens' surrender to Sparta in 404 BCE; the Peace of Nicias (421 BCE) as a mid-war pause

Classical culture: philosophy (Socrates c. 470-399 BCE, Plato c. 428-348 BCE, Aristotle 384-322 BCE); history-writing (Herodotus, 'Father of History'; Thucydides); drama (tragedy and comedy); and monumental art such as the Parthenon built under Pericles

The rise of Macedon under Philip II (dominant in Greece by 338 BCE) and Alexander the Great (356-323 BCE), and the Hellenistic era (323-31 BCE) in which Greek culture spread across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East
supporting: Pericles led Athens at the height of its power in the mid-fifth century and died in 429 BCE during the plague early in the Peloponnesian War

Alexander defeated the Persians at Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (330 BCE) and died at Babylon in 323 BCE; his successors founded Greek cities including Alexandria in Egypt, a center of Greek science and its famous library
Athenian democracy was direct (citizens voted in person in the Assembly) rather than representative, and the citizen body was on the order of 30,000-40,000 adult males in the Classical period

Greek achievement should be presented without triumphalism: contemporaneous civilizations — Achaemenid Persia, the Maurya empire in India, and Zhou-era (Warring States) China — were equally sophisticated

claims.claim: Classical Greece refers to the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, conventionally running from the end of the Persian Wars (479 BCE) to the death of Alexander the Great (323 BCE); the period's achievements were bound up with the Greek city-states' success in resisting two Persian invasions.

The basic political unit of the Greek world was the polis, an independent, self-governing city-state, typically centered on a fortified hill (acropolis) with its own government and cults; Athens developed a democracy while Sparta was an oligarchy headed by two kings with a rigidly militarized society in which boys were taken from their families at age seven to be raised by the state.

The reforms of Cleisthenes (c. 508 BCE) reorganized Athenian citizens into demes, trittyes, and ten tribes and created a Council of 500 (boule) in which male citizens had an equal right to speak, laying the foundation of Athenian democracy.

Athenian democracy was a direct democracy in which all adult male citizens could participate in government, but it was a limited democracy: women, enslaved people, and foreign residents (metics) could not participate. The Classical-period citizen body was on the order of thirty to forty thousand adult males.

In the Greco-Persian Wars, Greek forces defeated the Persians at Marathon (490 BCE), delayed them at Thermopylae and destroyed their fleet at Salamis (480 BCE), and defeated them decisively at Plataea (479 BCE); afterward Athens led the Delian League, formed in 477 BCE. (OpenStax dates the wars overall to 492-449 BCE.)

The Peloponnesian War began in 431 BCE between Athens (and its empire) and Sparta (and its allies); after a mid-war pause marked by the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE, the war resumed and ended when Athens surrendered to Sparta in 404 BCE. Sparta won.
Pericles led Athens at the height of its power in the mid-fifth century and died in 429 BCE during the plague that struck the city early in the Peloponnesian War.

Classical Greece produced influential philosophy (Socrates, c. 470-399 BCE, executed in Athens in 399 BCE; Plato, c. 428-348 BCE; Aristotle, 384-322 BCE, who tutored Alexander), the first works of critical history-writing (Herodotus, called the 'Father of History,' and Thucydides), and drama in the forms of tragedy and comedy.

By 338 BCE the kingdom of Macedon under Philip II had become the ruling power in Greece; his son Alexander the Great (356-323 BCE) conquered the Persian Empire, defeating it at Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (330 BCE) and reaching central Asia and India before dying at Babylon in 323 BCE.

The Hellenistic period ran from Alexander's death in 323 BCE to the Roman conquest of the last Hellenistic kingdom in 31 BCE; during it Greek language and culture spread across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East through new Greek cities such as Alexandria in Egypt, a center of Greek science and its great library, while new philosophies including Epicureanism and Stoicism arose.

Greek accomplishments should be presented without triumphalism: contemporaneous civilizations elsewhere — Achaemenid Persia, the Maurya empire in India, and Zhou-era China — were equally sophisticated, and Athenian democracy was far from universal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact span of the Classical period and of the Greco-Persian Wars is a matter of convention, not a single agreed date.
positions: The Classical period is commonly dated from the end of the Persian Wars (479 BCE) or the year 480 BCE to the death of Alexander (323 BCE); some texts begin it around 500 BCE.
The Greco-Persian Wars are dated 492-449 BCE by OpenStax, while other accounts begin them with the Ionian Revolt in 499 BCE; the decisive mainland battles fall in 490 and 480-479 BCE either way.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the period as 'roughly the fifth and fourth centuries BCE' anchored to 479 BCE and 323 BCE, presents the individual battle dates (which are secure), and attributes the 492-449 BCE span for the wars to OpenStax rather than stating it as the only possible framing.

sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports that the Hellenistic Period begins in 323 BCE with Alexander's death and ends in 31 BCE with Rome's conquest of the last Hellenistic kingdom, and that Alexander's conquests spread Greek culture and prompted a new wave of Greek colonization, especially in Asia. sourceRecords.title: Cleisthenes
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports that Cleisthenes' reforms (c. 508 BCE) established democracy in Athens by reorganizing citizens into 139 demes grouped into 30 trittyes and 10 tribes, reducing the power of traditional kinship groups, and by opening the new Council of 500 (boule) to male citizens with an equal right to speak; the article specifies participation was for 'males only.'
